edibilityNotes: Edible ONLY when thoroughly cooked. Raw or undercooked specimens are toxic and commonly cause gastrointestinal upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea). Even when fully cooked, a notable minority of people experience GI distress, so first-time eaters should try only a small, well-cooked portion and wait at least 24 hours before eating more. Discard the tough, fibrous stems and eat only the caps. CRITICAL: positively distinguish from the deadly amatoxin-containing Galerina marginata (rusty-brown spore print, ring, grows clustered on wood) and the toxic Hypholoma fasciculare (purple-brown spore print, bitter taste, sulphur-yellow gills), both of which also grow in clusters on wood. Always confirm a WHITE spore print before consuming.
description: Armillaria mellea, the Honey Fungus, is an aggressive parasitic and saprotrophic root-rot pathogen of trees and woody plants, and one of the most economically damaging forest and orchard pathogens worldwide. It fruits in dense, honey-colored to tawny-brown clusters at the base of living trunks, on stumps, and over buried roots, typically in autumn. Caps are 3-15 cm, convex becoming flattened, honey-yellow to reddish-brown, often with fine dark fibrillose scales concentrated toward the center; the flesh is white. Gills are whitish, becoming pinkish to rust-stained with age, attached to slightly decurrent. The stem bears a prominent persistent whitish to yellowish cottony ring. The spore print is white. Underground and beneath bark the fungus produces tough black shoestring-like rhizomorphs ("bootlaces") that spread infection from host to host, and its mycelium is bioluminescent, producing the faint green glow known as foxfire. It is edible only after thorough cooking; raw or undercooked material is toxic.
hosts: a wide range of woody trees and shrubs
distribution: Widespread across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, including Europe, North America, and Asia. The name Armillaria mellea has historically been applied broadly; molecular work has split the older "honey fungus" species complex into several distinct species, so some regional records may refer to closely related Armillaria taxa.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Galerina marginata
dangerousLookalikes.note: DEADLY. Contains amatoxins (the same class of toxins as the death cap). Also grows in clusters on wood. Distinguished by a rusty-brown to ochre spore print (vs. white in Armillaria), smaller size, smooth (non-scaly) brown to honey-brown cap, and a thinner stem. Confirming a white spore print is essential before eating any honey fungus.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hypholoma fasciculare
dangerousLookalikes.note: Toxic (severe GI upset). Sulphur Tuft. Clusters on stumps and wood. Distinguished by sulphur-yellow to greenish-yellow gills, a purple-brown to blackish spore print, intensely bitter taste, lack of a true ring, and absence of dark cap scales.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Pholiota species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Some Pholiota also cluster on wood with scaly caps and superficially resemble honey fungus; they typically have brown to rusty-brown spore prints rather than white, and many are slimy/viscid when moist.
